boilingPoint: 337 °C at 1 atm (concentrated); forms aerosol in atmosphere
odor: Pungent, acrid at high concentrations; odorless when dilute
environmentalPersistence: Low as free acid — rapidly neutralized by soil buffers; but sulfate ion persists and acidifies over time

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate — acid-induced nutrient lockout and root damage reduces growth
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Moderate to strong — cuticle damage causes loss of structural integrity
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Moderate — membrane damage and root acid injury impair water uptake
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Moderate-strong — H⁺ displaces Mg²⁺ from chlorophyll; nutrient lockout
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Strong — acid burn causes immediate tissue death on contact; characteristic interveinal necrotic lesions
morphologicalEffects.pigmentation: Minimal — acid damage overwhelms defense pigmentation
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Moderately to severely inhibited — soil acidification disrupts mineral nutrition
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Both affected by foliar spray; old leaves show pH-induced chlorosis first from soil route

physiologyEffects.chlorophyllReduction: Strong — Mg²⁺ displacement from chlorophyll porphyrin ring
physiologyEffects.stomatalConductance: Strongly reduced — cuticle and guard cell damage
physiologyEffects.waterUptake: Impaired by root damage in acidified soil
physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Strongly disrupted — soil acidification immobilizes Ca, Mg, K; mobilizes toxic Al and Mn
physiologyEffects.membranePermeability: Strongly increased — acid directly denatures membrane proteins

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Strong — acid-induced membrane damage generates ROS cascade
molecularEffects.anthocyaninInduction: Minimal — acid damage is too rapid for defense induction

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Strong — soil acidification is one of the most powerful microbiome disruptors
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Strongly suppressed — acid-sensitive PGPR and nitrogen-fixers most affected
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Acid-tolerant fungi (e.g. some Aspergillus) may increase; mycorrhizal associations disrupted

firstSymptoms: leaf surface bleaching at contact points
temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: Poor for contact damage; soil pH recovery possible over weeks if liming applied

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Immediate bleaching/whitening at contact → necrotic brown; background chlorosis
visualSimulation.firstAffectedRegion: Leaf surface (contact points) for foliar; roots for soil delivery
visualSimulation.damageSpread: Contact zones first; then interveinal spread
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Irregular bleached patches (acid burn) with interveinal chlorosis — distinctive acid rain pattern
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — sulfate and malate pH stress signature
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Strongly reduced; acid-tolerant pathogen fraction rises
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: Bleached contact zones remain; new growth may be healthy if soil pH recovers

synergies.synergyNote: The actual acid rain mixture — H₂SO₄ + HNO₃ + SO₂ + NO₂ together create the real-world acid rain scenario; sulfate and nitrate together acidify soil faster than either alone and compound cuticle damage

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Coal and oil combustion SO₂ → atmospheric oxidation to H₂SO₄; industrial emissions; volcanic eruptions
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Dilute sulfuric acid used in soil pH adjustment; concentrated form — industrial only
educationalContext.humanToxicity: High — severe burns to skin/eyes/respiratory tract; concentrated form is one of the most dangerous industrial chemicals
educationalContext.climateLink: Acid rain directly caused by fossil fuel combustion — one of the most direct links between industrial activity and ecosystem damage
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Acid rain killing forests in 1970s–80s was one of the first major environmental crises to generate public awareness and policy change — the Clean Air Act story is directly teachable
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Acid rain, forest die-off, lake acidification, Clean Air Act history

sources: Kozlowski TT, Constantinidou HA (1986). Responses of woody plants to environmental pollution. The Botanical Review, 52(4), 311–382.
Likens GE, Bormann FH (1974). Acid rain: a serious regional environmental problem. Science, 184(4142), 1176–1179.
Cape JN (1993). Direct damage to vegetation caused by acid rain and polluted cloud: definition of critical levels for forest trees. Environmental Pollution, 82(2), 167–180.
